decks.title: The Supreme Court — Part 1: Composition, Appointment, Removal and Independence
goals: State the composition of the Supreme Court and the qualifications of its judges
Describe how judges are appointed and removed
Explain the provisions that keep the judiciary independent of the executive and the legislature

slides.heading: The Supreme Court of India
slides.body_md: Part 1 — who sits on the **Supreme Court**, how they are **appointed** and **removed**, and why the Court is **independent**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the Supreme Court's place in the court system, who sits on it, how judges are appointed and removed, and why the Court is independent
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: When two States quarrel, or a citizen's rights are taken away, the final word lies with one court: the Supreme Court of India. In this part we look at who sits on that court, how judges are chosen, how a judge can be removed, and the safeguards that let judges decide cases without fear of the government or of Parliament.

slides.heading: One integrated judiciary
slides.body_md: India has a **single** system of courts, with the **Supreme Court** at the top.

visual.caption: One integrated judiciary for the whole country.

slides.narration: Unlike some federations, India does not have separate Union and State court systems. There is one ladder. District and Sessions Courts are at the bottom of the ladder shown here, High Courts stand at the top in each State, and the Supreme Court is at the apex for the whole country. Appeals move up the ladder, and the law declared by the Supreme Court binds every court below it.

slides.heading: Quick check: the apex court
slides.body_md: Which court's rulings bind every other court in India?
slides.narration: Look again at the ladder of courts. Which court stands at the very top?

slides.heading: Composition of the Supreme Court
slides.body_md: A **Chief Justice** and up to **33** other judges: **34** in all (as of 2024).

rows: Chief Justice of India and up to 33 other judges (34 in all, as of 2024)
Delhi, or other places fixed by the Chief Justice with the President's approval

visual.alt: Table of the Supreme Court's composition: set up by Article 124; the Chief Justice and up to 33 other judges, 34 in all as of 2024; strength fixed by Parliament; sits in Delhi; judges retire at 65

slides.narration: The Constitution sets up the Supreme Court in Article one hundred and twenty-four. Parliament decides the number of judges by law. Since a law of twenty nineteen, the Court may have the Chief Justice of India and up to thirty-three other judges, thirty-four in all. The Court normally sits in Delhi. Its judges retire when they complete sixty-five years of age.

slides.heading: Who can become a judge?
slides.body_md: Citizenship plus **one** of three routes.

rows: At least 5 years as a judge of a High Court
At least 10 years as an advocate of a High Court
A distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President

visual.alt: Table of qualifications for a Supreme Court judge: an Indian citizen who has been a High Court judge for 5 years, or an advocate of a High Court for 10 years, or a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion

slides.narration: A judge must be a citizen of India. Beyond that there are three routes. The person may have served at least five years as a judge of a High Court, or practised at least ten years as an advocate of a High Court, or be a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President. Notice that there is no minimum age, only the retirement age.

slides.heading: How judges are appointed
slides.body_md: The **President** appoints; the names come from a **collegium** of senior judges.

nodes.label: Collegium of the Chief Justice and senior-most judges recommends names
President signs the warrant of appointment
Senior-most judge usually appointed Chief Justice

visual.alt: Flow of appointment: the collegium of the Chief Justice and senior-most judges recommends names, the government processes them, the President signs the warrant, and the senior-most judge is usually appointed Chief Justice
visual.caption: Practice shaped by Supreme Court judgments in the 1990s; a 2014 commission was struck down in 2015.

slides.narration: The Constitution says the President appoints the judges after consultation. Supreme Court judgments in the nineteen nineties interpreted this to mean that a collegium, the Chief Justice and the senior-most judges, recommends names. A law of twenty fourteen tried to create a commission for appointments, but the Court struck it down in twenty fifteen, so the collegium practice continues. The senior-most judge is usually made Chief Justice.

slides.heading: Quick check: the 2015 decision
slides.body_md: Which body for appointing judges did the Court strike down in 2015?
slides.narration: A new body for choosing judges was created in twenty fourteen and struck down the next year. Can you name it?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: who qualifies?
slides.body_md: Test four imagined candidates against the three routes.
bullets: Step 1: is the person a **citizen**?
Step 2: which **route**: High Court judge, advocate, or jurist?
Step 3: are the **years** enough?

rows: 12 years as an advocate of a High Court
3 years as a High Court judge, no other service
7 years as a High Court judge
8 years as an advocate in a District Court only

visual.alt: Worked example table: Meenakshi with 12 years at the High Court bar qualifies; Joseph with 3 years as a High Court judge does not; Farida with 7 years as a High Court judge qualifies; Arvind with 8 years only in a District Court does not
visual.caption: Check the route and the number of years.

slides.narration: Let us test four imagined candidates. Meenakshi has practised twelve years at a High Court bar, more than the ten needed, so she qualifies. Joseph has been a High Court judge for only three years, less than five. Farida has seven years on a High Court bench, so she qualifies. Arvind has practised only in a District Court, which is not a High Court, so he does not qualify.

slides.heading: Removal of a judge
slides.body_md: Only for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**, by **both Houses** and the **President**.

nodes.label: Charge of proved misbehaviour or incapacity
Motion admitted in a House of Parliament
Each House passes an address by the special majority

visual.alt: Flow of removal of a judge: a charge of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, a motion admitted in a House, an inquiry committee, an address passed in each House by the special majority, and the President's order
visual.caption: Both Houses, same session.

slides.narration: A judge cannot be removed for an unpopular judgment. The only grounds are proved misbehaviour or incapacity. A motion is moved in a House of Parliament and an inquiry committee examines the charge. If it is proved, each House must pass an address by a special majority in the same session. The address goes to the President, who then orders the removal.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting the votes
slides.body_md: Two conditions in **each** House: a majority of the **total membership** and **two-thirds of members present and voting**.

visual.alt: Worked example table: in a Lok Sabha of 543, 330 of 480 present vote yes, meeting both 272 and 320, so it passes; in a Rajya Sabha of 245, 131 of 210 vote yes, above 123 but below 140, so it fails
visual.caption: Imagined votes; both conditions must hold in each House.

slides.narration: Here are imagined votes. In a Lok Sabha of five hundred and forty-three, three hundred and thirty members vote yes out of four hundred and eighty present. That is more than half the whole House and at least two-thirds of those voting, so it passes. In the Rajya Sabha, one hundred and thirty-one yes votes out of two hundred and ten present clears half the House but falls short of two-thirds, so the motion fails.

slides.heading: Quick check: retirement
slides.body_md: Up to what age does a Supreme Court judge hold office?
slides.narration: Supreme Court judges and High Court judges retire at different ages. Which one belongs to the Supreme Court?

slides.heading: Why independence matters
slides.body_md: The Court often decides cases **against the government**; judges must be free of pressure.

nodes.label: Salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund and not reducible
Conduct not discussed in Parliament except for removal

visual.alt: Flow listing six safeguards of judicial independence: security of tenure until sixty-five, salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund and not reducible, no discussion of conduct in Parliament except for removal, power to punish for contempt, no practice after retirement, and separation from the executive
visual.caption: Six safeguards.

slides.narration: The Supreme Court settles disputes in which the government itself is a party, and it protects the rights of citizens against the State. If judges feared losing their jobs or their pay, they might lean towards the government. So the Constitution builds in safeguards: security of tenure, protected salaries, protection from debate in Parliament, the contempt power, a ban on practice after retirement, and separation from the executive.

slides.heading: Tenure, salary and authority
columns:
**Tenure and salary**

- Office until **65**; removal only by the hard procedure.
- Salaries **charged on the Consolidated Fund**; not voted on yearly.
- Cannot be **reduced** after appointment, except in a **financial emergency**.

**Conduct and authority**

- Parliament **cannot discuss** a judge's conduct except during removal (**Article 121**).
- Court can **punish for contempt** (**Article 129**).
- Retired judges **cannot practise** in any court in India.

rows: Judges need not fear losing office for a judgment
Pay does not depend on a yearly vote
Judges are not attacked in Parliament
No temptation to please future clients
Executive officers do not act as judges

visual.alt: Table of safeguards of judicial independence with their source and purpose: tenure (Article 124), salary (Article 125 and the Consolidated Fund), no discussion of conduct (Article 121), contempt power (Article 129), no practice after retirement (Article 124) and separation from the executive (Article 50)

slides.narration: Think of the safeguards in two groups. The first protects the judge personally: a fixed tenure until sixty-five, and a salary that is charged on the Consolidated Fund, so it is not voted on every year and cannot be cut after appointment except in a financial emergency. The second protects the Court's authority: no debate on a judge's conduct in Parliament, the power to punish contempt, and no practice after retirement.

slides.heading: Quick check: debate in Parliament
slides.body_md: When may Parliament discuss a judge's conduct?
slides.narration: Parliament is free to debate almost anything, but there is one limit concerning judges. When is their conduct open to discussion?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Supreme Court: Chief Justice and up to **33** other judges; seat in Delhi.
Qualifications: citizen plus High Court judge 5 years, advocate 10 years, or distinguished jurist.
Appointment by the President; names from the collegium.
Removal: proved misbehaviour or incapacity; special majority in both Houses.
Independence: tenure, salary, no discussion, contempt power, no later practice, separation.

nodes.label: Chief Justice and up to 33 judges
Appointed by the President on the collegium's recommendation
Removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity by both Houses
Independence protected by tenure, salary and other safeguards

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: the Chief Justice and up to 33 other judges; appointment by the President on the collegium's recommendation; removal only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity by both Houses; independence protected by tenure, salary and other safeguards
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. The Supreme Court has a Chief Justice and up to thirty-three other judges. A judge must be a citizen with five years on a High Court bench, ten years at a High Court bar, or be a distinguished jurist. The President appoints judges on the collegium's advice. Removal needs proved misbehaviour or incapacity and a special majority in both Houses. Many safeguards protect independence.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Removal needs **both** a majority of the total membership **and** two-thirds of members present and voting, in **each** House.
Supreme Court judges retire at **65**; High Court judges at **62**.
Do not write "impeachment" grounds for judges: it is **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
For independence, give **provisions**, not just the word "independent".
10-mark answers: one clear point for each mark in each part.
slides.narration: Some tips. For removal, mention both conditions of the special majority, and say it applies in each House. Keep the retirement ages apart: sixty-five for the Supreme Court and sixty-two for High Courts. Write proved misbehaviour or incapacity as the grounds. When asked about independence, name the actual provisions. And give one clear point for every mark.

decks.title: The Supreme Court — Part 2: Jurisdiction, Judicial Review and Writs
goals: Distinguish original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction with examples
Explain review of its own judgments, judicial review and the Court of Record
Name the five writs and state the purpose of each

slides.heading: What the Supreme Court can do
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the Court's **jurisdictions**, **judicial review** and the **writs** that protect Fundamental Rights.

nodes.label: Review, judicial review and Court of Record

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction; review of its own judgments, judicial review and Court of Record; and writs for Fundamental Rights
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Jurisdiction means the kinds of cases a court may hear. In this part we sort the Supreme Court's work into original, appellate and advisory jurisdiction, look at its power to review its own judgments, its role as a Court of Record and its power of judicial review, and finally meet the five writs that make Fundamental Rights real.

slides.heading: The Court's main jurisdictions
slides.body_md: Original, writ, appellate and advisory, plus review and Court of Record.

visual.caption: Four main jurisdictions, and more.

slides.narration: This hub shows the Court's main kinds of work. Some cases begin in the Supreme Court itself: that is original jurisdiction, and writ petitions for Fundamental Rights also start here. Some come on appeal from High Courts: appellate jurisdiction. The President may seek its opinion: advisory jurisdiction. It can also review its own judgments, and it is a Court of Record.

slides.heading: Original jurisdiction
slides.body_md: **Article 131:** disputes between the **Union** and **States**, or between **States**, begin here.

visual.alt: Table of disputes within original jurisdiction under Article 131: the Union against one or more States, the Union and some States against other States, and one State against another
visual.caption: Article 131: these cases begin in the Supreme Court.

slides.narration: Original jurisdiction covers cases that start in the Supreme Court and nowhere else. Under Article one hundred and thirty-one, these are disputes between the Union and one or more States, between the Union and some States on one side and other States on the other, and between two or more States. As a federal umpire, the Court keeps the balance between the Union and the States.

slides.heading: Quick check: what original means
slides.body_md: What does original jurisdiction mean?
slides.narration: Remember the meaning of original here. Where does such a case begin?

slides.heading: Appellate jurisdiction
slides.body_md: Appeals from **High Courts**: constitutional, civil and criminal; and **special leave**.

rows: A High Court certifies a substantial question about interpreting the Constitution
A High Court certifies a substantial question of law of general importance
For example, a High Court reverses an acquittal and passes a death sentence
The Supreme Court allows an appeal from almost any court or tribunal, except armed forces tribunals

visual.alt: Table of appellate jurisdiction: constitutional appeals on a certificate about interpreting the Constitution; civil appeals on a certificate of a substantial question of general importance; criminal appeals such as when a High Court reverses an acquittal and passes a death sentence; and special leave under Article 136 from almost any court or tribunal except armed forces tribunals

slides.narration: Most cases reach the Supreme Court on appeal. Constitutional appeals come when a High Court certifies a substantial question about interpreting the Constitution. Civil appeals need a substantial question of general importance. In criminal cases, an appeal lies for example when a High Court reverses an acquittal and passes a death sentence. Under Article one hundred and thirty-six, the Court may also grant special leave to appeal from almost any court.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which jurisdiction?
slides.body_md: Sort four imagined matters.
bullets: Does the case **begin** in the Supreme Court? Original.
Does it come **from a High Court**? Appellate.
Is the **President** asking a question? Advisory.
Is the Court looking at **its own** judgment? Review.

rows: Two States quarrel over a border mine
A death sentence passed after a High Court reverses an acquittal
The President asks if a proposed law would be valid
A party shows an obvious error in the Court's own judgment

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting imagined matters: a border dispute between States is original; an appeal against a death sentence after reversal of acquittal is appellate; the President's question is advisory; an obvious error in the Court's own judgment is review
visual.caption: Ask where the case starts and who brings it.

slides.narration: Let us sort four imagined matters. Two States quarrelling over a mine on their border start in the Supreme Court, so that is original jurisdiction. A death sentence passed after a High Court reverses an acquittal comes up on appeal. A question from the President is advisory. And a party pointing out an obvious error in the Court's own judgment asks for review under Article one hundred and thirty-seven.

slides.heading: Advisory jurisdiction
slides.body_md: **Article 143:** only the **President** can ask; the Court's opinion **guides** but does not **bind** like a judgment.

nodes.label: Question of law or fact of public importance
Opinion guides; not binding like a judgment

visual.alt: Flow of advisory jurisdiction: a question of public importance, reference by the President under Article 143, hearing by the Court, its opinion, which guides but is not binding like a judgment
visual.caption: Only the President can refer.

slides.narration: Sometimes the President needs legal advice before acting. Under Article one hundred and forty-three, the President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court. The Court hears the matter and gives its opinion. This opinion guides the government, but it is not a judgment in a dispute and does not bind in the same way.

slides.heading: Quick check: who may ask?
slides.body_md: True or false: any citizen may seek an advisory opinion.
slides.narration: Only one person may make a reference for an advisory opinion. Can an ordinary citizen do it?

slides.heading: Review, Court of Record and binding law
slides.body_md: Article **137** (review), **129** (Court of Record), **141** (law binding on all courts).

rows: Reconsiders its own decision, for example to correct an obvious error
Its records are evidence and precedent; can punish for contempt
Every court in India follows the law it declares

visual.alt: Table of three powers: review of its own judgments under Article 137, Court of Record under Article 129 with records as evidence and the contempt power, and Article 141 making its law binding on all courts

slides.narration: Three more powers complete the picture. Under Article one hundred and thirty-seven, the Court may review its own judgment, for example to correct an obvious error. Under Article one hundred and twenty-nine, it is a Court of Record: its records are evidence and precedent, and it can punish for contempt. Under Article one hundred and forty-one, the law it declares binds all courts in India.

slides.heading: Judicial review
slides.body_md: The power to declare laws and orders **void** if they violate the **Constitution**.

nodes.label: A law or an order is challenged
Court compares it with the Constitution
Inconsistent: declared void to that extent

visual.alt: Flow of judicial review: a law or order is challenged, the Court compares it with the Constitution, and it stands if consistent or is declared void to the extent it is inconsistent
visual.caption: Guardian of the Constitution.

slides.narration: Judicial review is the power to test laws and government orders against the Constitution. When a law is challenged, the Court compares it with the Constitution. If it fits, it stands. If it takes away Fundamental Rights beyond what the Constitution allows, or if the Union or a State has gone beyond its powers, the Court declares it void to that extent. This makes the Court the guardian of the Constitution.

slides.heading: Quick check: an error in a judgment
slides.body_md: Which power lets the Court look again at its own decision?
slides.narration: The Court has delivered a judgment, but a party shows an obvious error in it. Which power can the Court use?

slides.heading: The five writs
slides.body_md: **Article 32** lets citizens go straight to the Supreme Court; the remedy is itself a **Fundamental Right**.

rows: Produce a detained person; test the detention
Order a public authority to do its legal duty
Stop a lower court before it exceeds its jurisdiction
Quash an order already passed without jurisdiction
Test a person's right to hold a public office

visual.alt: Table of the five writs with their literal sense and purpose: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto

slides.narration: Rights mean little without a way to enforce them. Article thirty-two lets a person go directly to the Supreme Court, and this remedy is itself a Fundamental Right. The Court may issue five writs. Habeas corpus brings a detained person before the court. Mandamus commands a public authority to do its duty. Prohibition and certiorari control lower courts. Quo warranto tests the right to hold a public office.

slides.heading: Prohibition or certiorari?
slides.body_md: The difference is **timing**: before the decision, or after it.

nodes.label: Case pending in a lower tribunal

visual.alt: Flow contrasting prohibition and certiorari: while a case is pending in a lower tribunal, prohibition stops it from exceeding its jurisdiction; after an order is passed without jurisdiction, certiorari quashes it
visual.caption: Prohibition prevents; certiorari cures.

slides.narration: Prohibition and certiorari both deal with lower courts and tribunals that go beyond their powers. The difference is timing. Prohibition is issued while the case is still pending, to stop the tribunal from going ahead. Certiorari is issued after the order is passed, to quash it. A simple way to remember: prohibition prevents, certiorari cures.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: choose the writ
slides.body_md: Match the problem to the writ.
bullets: Detention? **Habeas corpus**.
Duty refused? **Mandamus**.
Unqualified office-holder? **Quo warranto**.
Order already passed beyond powers? **Certiorari**.

rows: A labourer held by police for a week without being produced before a magistrate
An officer will not register a birth the law requires him to register
An unqualified person holds the chair of a public board
A tribunal has already decided a case outside its powers

visual.alt: Worked example table choosing writs for imagined problems: unlawful detention needs habeas corpus, refusal of a legal duty needs mandamus, an unqualified office-holder needs quo warranto, and a decision already made beyond powers needs certiorari

slides.narration: Let us choose writs for four imagined problems. A labourer held by the police for a week without being produced before a magistrate needs habeas corpus. An officer refusing to register a birth needs mandamus. An unqualified person chairing a public board can be challenged by quo warranto. sections.heading: 1. Composition and qualifications

- Established by **Article 124**; **Chief Justice of India** and up to **33** other judges (**34** in all, as of 2024; number fixed by Parliament by law).
- Sits in **Delhi** (or elsewhere as the Chief Justice decides with the President's approval).
- **Qualifications:** citizen of India and either a **High Court judge for 5 years**, or an **advocate of a High Court for 10 years**, or a **distinguished jurist** in the President's opinion.
- **Tenure:** until **65**; may resign by writing to the President.

sections.heading: 2. Appointment and removal
sections.body_md:
- **Appointment:** by the **President**; in practice on the recommendation of a **collegium** (Chief Justice and senior-most judges), a practice shaped by Supreme Court judgments in **1993** and **1998**. The **NJAC** (99th Amendment and law of 2014) was **struck down in 2015**. The senior-most judge is usually appointed Chief Justice.
- **Removal:** only for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**. Motion in a House, **inquiry committee**, then an **address** passed in **each House** by a **majority of its total membership** and **two-thirds of members present and voting**, in the same session; the **President** orders removal.

A formal resolution of a House presented to the President.

sections.heading: 3. Independence of the judiciary
sections.body_md:
- **Security of tenure** until 65; difficult removal.
- **Salaries** charged on the **Consolidated Fund**; **cannot be reduced** after appointment except in a **financial emergency**.
- **Article 121:** no discussion of a judge's conduct in Parliament except on a removal motion.
- **Article 129:** power to **punish for contempt**.
- **No practice** in any court in India after retirement.
- **Article 50:** separation of the judiciary from the executive.

key_terms.definition_md: The main account of the Union government; expenditure charged on it is not voted on every year.
Disobeying or showing disrespect to a court in a way that lowers its authority.

sections.body_md:

- **Appellate:** **constitutional** (certificate of a substantial question about the Constitution), **civil** (substantial question of general importance), **criminal** (for example, death sentence after a High Court reverses an acquittal); **special leave (Article 136)** from any court or tribunal except armed forces tribunals.
- **Advisory (Article 143):** the **President** may refer a question of law or fact of public importance; the opinion **guides** but does not bind like a judgment.

key_terms.definition_md: The authority of a court to hear and decide particular kinds of cases.
Permission given by the Supreme Court itself to appeal.

sections.heading: 5. Review, judicial review and Court of Record
sections.body_md:
- **Review (Article 137):** the Court may reconsider its **own** judgment, e.g. for an error apparent on the record.
- **Judicial review:** the power to declare **laws and executive actions void** if they violate the **Constitution**; protects **Fundamental Rights** and the **federal** division of powers.
- **Court of Record (Article 129):** records are **evidence and precedent**; power to **punish for contempt**.
- **Article 141:** law declared by the Supreme Court **binds all courts** in India.

key_terms.definition_md: Testing laws and orders against the Constitution and striking down those that conflict with it.
A court whose records are permanent evidence and which can punish for contempt.

Court compares it with the Constitution

Its records are evidence and precedent; can punish for contempt

sections.heading: 6. Writs for Fundamental Rights
sections.body_md:
- **Article 32:** right to move the Supreme Court for enforcing Fundamental Rights; itself a **Fundamental Right**.
- **Habeas corpus:** produce a detained person.
- **Mandamus:** command a public authority to do its duty.
- **Prohibition:** stop a lower court **before** it exceeds its jurisdiction.
- **Certiorari:** quash an order **already passed** without jurisdiction.
- **Quo warranto:** test the right to hold a **public office**.

key_terms.definition_md: A written order of a superior court commanding or forbidding an action.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing "impeachment" for the removal of a judge, or giving "violation of the Constitution" as the ground.
- Giving only one of the two conditions of the special majority.
- Saying any citizen can seek an advisory opinion.
- Mixing up prohibition (before) and certiorari (after).
- Confusing review of the Court's own judgments with judicial review.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one point per mark; the last part often asks for an explanation, a comparison or a judgement.

questions.stem_md: What is the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court of India, counting the Chief Justice (as of 2024)?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 34. Parliament fixes the number of judges by law; since a 2019 Act the Court may have the Chief Justice and up to 33 other judges, so 34 in all. Thirty-one was the earlier figure; 25 and 45 are not the present strength.

questions.stem_md: A student asks who has the power to increase the number of judges of the Supreme Court. Which answer is correct?

options.text_md: The Chief Justice, by an order of the Court
The President, by an ordinance only
The States, by a resolution of their Assemblies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Parliament, by passing a law. The Constitution allows Parliament to prescribe the number of judges by law, which is how the strength has been raised over the years. The Chief Justice and the States cannot change it, and it is not done only by ordinance.

questions.stem_md: Advocate Meenakshi, an imagined lawyer, has practised for twelve years in a High Court. Is she qualified to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court?

options.text_md: Yes, because 10 years as an advocate of a High Court is one of the qualifications
No, because only serving High Court judges can be appointed
No, because she must first serve fifteen years as a district judge
Yes, but only as an acting judge for one year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Yes, because 10 years as an advocate of a High Court is one of the qualifications. A citizen who has been an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years qualifies (with citizenship). Being a High Court judge for 5 years, or a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion, are the other routes. The other options invent conditions.

questions.stem_md: Apart from service as a High Court judge or as an advocate, which third route to the Supreme Court bench does the Constitution allow?

options.text_md: Being a member of Parliament for ten years
Being nominated by a State Governor
Being a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President
Passing a special examination held by the Court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Being a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President. A citizen who is, in the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist may also be appointed. Membership of Parliament, nomination by a Governor and an examination are not routes to the Court.

questions.stem_md: Up to what age does a judge of the Supreme Court hold office?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 65 years. Supreme Court judges retire on completing 65. Sixty-two is the retirement age for High Court judges; sixty and seventy are not constitutional figures here.

questions.stem_md: Under the Constitution, which authority formally appoints the judges of the Supreme Court?

options.text_md: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The President. Judges are appointed by the President by warrant under hand and seal. In practice the recommendations come from a collegium of senior judges; the Prime Minister, the Speaker and the Law Minister do not appoint judges themselves.

questions.stem_md: The practice by which a group of the senior-most judges recommends names for appointment to the Supreme Court grew out of which development?

options.text_md: A resolution of the Rajya Sabha in 1985
An order of the Election Commission
Judgments of the Supreme Court in the 1990s interpreting "consultation" (the Second and Third Judges cases)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Judgments of the Supreme Court in the 1990s interpreting "consultation" (the Second and Third Judges cases). The collegium practice was shaped by Supreme Court judgments in 1993 and 1998 (often called the Second and Third Judges cases). It was not created by an amendment in 1950, a Rajya Sabha resolution or the Election Commission.

questions.stem_md: A body proposed by a 2014 amendment to recommend appointments of judges was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015. What was it called?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The National Judicial Appointments Commission. The National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) was created by the 99th Amendment and a law of 2014, and the Court held them invalid in 2015, so the collegium practice continued. The other commissions have unrelated roles.

questions.stem_md: On which grounds can a judge of the Supreme Court be removed from office?

options.text_md: Delivering a judgment against the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The only grounds are proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Judgments against the government or disagreements cannot be grounds, and retirement is at 65, not removal at 60.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Lok Sabha of 543 members, 480 members are present and voting on a motion to remove a judge, and 330 vote in favour. Does the motion meet the required majority in this House?

options.text_md: No: it needs two-thirds of the total membership, that is 362
Yes: 330 is more than half of 543 and at least two-thirds of 480
No: it needs a simple majority of members present only
Yes: any majority of members present is enough

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Yes: 330 is more than half of 543 and at least two-thirds of 480. The address must be supported by a majority of the total membership (at least 272 of 543) and by two-thirds of members present and voting (at least 320 of 480). 330 meets both. Two-thirds of the total membership is the rule for impeaching the President, not for removing a judge.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In an imagined Rajya Sabha of 245 members, a motion to remove a judge with 131 votes in favour and 210 members present and voting meets the required majority.
questions.solution_md: **False.** It fails. 131 is more than half of the total membership (123 needed), but two-thirds of 210 members present and voting is 140, and 131 is less than that. Both conditions must hold.

questions.stem_md: A judge of the Supreme Court retires on completing the age of ___ years.
questions.solution_md: The retirement age is 65 (sixty-five).

questions.stem_md: Put the steps for removing a Supreme Court judge in the correct order.

options.text_md: A committee investigates the charge of misbehaviour or incapacity
The address is presented to the President, who orders the removal
A motion is moved in a House of Parliament and admitted by the presiding officer
Each House passes an address by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (d) → (b). Motion and admission; investigation by a committee under the Judges (Inquiry) Act; passing of the address in both Houses in the same session with the special majority; order of the President.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State the qualifications a citizen needs to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court.
questions.solution_md: Citizenship plus any one of the three routes.

answer.model_answer_md: The person must be a **citizen of India** and must have been either a **High Court judge for 5 years**, or an **advocate of a High Court for 10 years**, or a **distinguished jurist** in the President's opinion.

marking_scheme.step: One of the three routes, correctly stated

questions.stem_md: How are the Chief Justice and the other judges of the Supreme Court appointed in practice?
questions.solution_md: Formal appointment by the President; recommendation by the collegium; seniority convention for the Chief Justice.

answer.model_answer_md: The **President** appoints them. In practice the names are **recommended by a collegium** of the Chief Justice and the senior-most judges, and the **senior-most judge** is usually appointed **Chief Justice**.

questions.stem_md: Explain the procedure for removing a judge of the Supreme Court, stating the grounds and the majority required.
questions.solution_md: Grounds; motion, inquiry and special majority in both Houses; the President's order.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The grounds are **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
2. A motion is moved in **either House**; after an **inquiry committee** finds the charge proved, **each House** must pass an **address** by a **majority of its total membership** and **two-thirds of members present and voting**, in the same session.
3. The address is presented to the **President**, who then **orders the removal**.

marking_scheme.step: Inquiry and special majority in each House

questions.stem_md: Why are the salaries of Supreme Court judges charged on the Consolidated Fund of India?

options.text_md: So that judges can raise their own salaries
So that the States pay the judges
So that they are not voted on by Parliament every year, which protects the judges from pressure
So that judges are paid only when the budget is passed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** So that they are not voted on by Parliament every year, which protects the judges from pressure. Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund is not subject to the annual vote of Parliament, so the judges do not depend on the goodwill of the legislature or the executive. Judges cannot fix their own pay, the States do not pay them, and payment does not wait for the budget vote.

questions.stem_md: An imagined government wants to reduce the salary of a serving Supreme Court judge because it dislikes a recent decision. What does the Constitution say?

options.text_md: Salaries can be cut at any time by an order of the Law Ministry
Salaries can be cut only by the Chief Justice
Salaries can be cut if the Lok Sabha passes a simple resolution
Salaries cannot be varied to the disadvantage of a judge after appointment, except during a financial emergency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Salaries cannot be varied to the disadvantage of a judge after appointment, except during a financial emergency. A judge's salary and allowances cannot be changed to the judge's disadvantage after appointment; the only exception is a financial emergency under Article 360. The other options would make judges dependent on the executive or legislature.

questions.stem_md: After retirement, a former judge of the Supreme Court wishes to appear as a lawyer in a District Court. What is the constitutional position?

options.text_md: He may appear in any court except the Supreme Court
He may appear only in High Courts
He may appear anywhere after five years
A retired Supreme Court judge cannot plead or act in any court or before any authority in India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A retired Supreme Court judge cannot plead or act in any court or before any authority in India. A person who has held office as a Supreme Court judge may not plead or act in any court or before any authority within India. This keeps sitting judges from being tempted by future practice. The other options invent exceptions.

questions.stem_md: When may Parliament discuss the conduct of a judge of the Supreme Court in the discharge of judicial duties?

options.text_md: Only on a motion for presenting an address for the judge's removal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Only on a motion for presenting an address for the judge's removal. Article 121 bars discussion of a judge's conduct in Parliament except on a motion for removal. Question Hour or a minister's request do not open such debate, and removal proceedings are the one allowed occasion.

questions.stem_md: An imagined newspaper repeatedly publishes false claims that a bench of the Supreme Court took bribes, without any evidence. Which power of the Court can it use to protect its authority?

options.text_md: Power to dissolve the Lok Sabha
Power to punish for contempt of court

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Power to punish for contempt of court. As a Court of Record, the Supreme Court can punish for contempt of itself, which protects its dignity and authority. Dissolving the Lok Sabha and issuing ordinances belong to the President; impeachment applies only to the President.

questions.stem_md: Which part of the Constitution directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State?

options.text_md: The Directive Principles of State Policy (Article 50)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Directive Principles of State Policy (Article 50). Article 50, a Directive Principle, asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive. The Fundamental Duties, the Seventh Schedule and the Preamble do not contain this direction.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Supreme Court judges can decide cases against the government without fear of losing their jobs.

**Reason (R):** Judges hold office until the age of 65 and can be removed only by a special procedure involving both Houses of Parliament.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both statements are true, and R explains A: security of tenure, with removal only by a difficult parliamentary procedure on proved misbehaviour or incapacity, frees judges to decide independently.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The salaries of Supreme Court judges are protected from cuts during their term, except during a financial emergency.

**Reason (R):** Parliament votes on the judges' salaries every year when it passes the budget.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: the salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and are not put to the annual vote of Parliament.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under the Constitution, a minister may direct a Supreme Court judge on how to decide a pending case if the case involves the government.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The judiciary is independent of the executive; no minister can direct a judge, and the separation of the judiciary from the executive is part of the constitutional scheme.

questions.stem_md: Mention two provisions concerning the pay and service of Supreme Court judges that keep them independent of the government.
questions.solution_md: Any two: salary protection, tenure, difficult removal, no practice after retirement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Their **salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund** and **cannot be reduced** after appointment (except in a financial emergency).
2. They have **security of tenure** until **65** and can be removed only by a **special procedure** in Parliament.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the ban on legal practice after retirement helps keep sitting judges impartial.
questions.solution_md: Link the ban to the absence of temptation during service.

answer.model_answer_md: A judge **cannot hope to earn later** by appearing for **clients or the government**, so there is **no temptation** to please future clients or officials **while deciding cases** today.

questions.stem_md: An imagined debating club argues that judges in India are free to decide cases fairly. Give three constitutional provisions they can cite to support this view.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct provisions, each explained briefly.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Security of tenure:** judges serve until **65** and are removed only on **proved misbehaviour or incapacity** by a special majority of **both Houses**.
2. **Financial security:** salaries are **charged on the Consolidated Fund** and **cannot be cut** after appointment except in a financial emergency.
3. **Protection of conduct and authority:** Parliament **cannot discuss** a judge's conduct except during removal, and the Court can **punish for contempt**.

marking_scheme.step: Another provision (no discussion, contempt, no practice, separation)

questions.stem_md: Two imagined States, Uttarvan and Dakshinpur, disagree about which of them may collect a tax on goods crossing their common border. In which jurisdiction would the Supreme Court hear this dispute directly?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Original jurisdiction. Disputes between two or more States (or between the Union and States) are heard by the Supreme Court in its original jurisdiction under Article 131: the case starts there. Appellate means hearing an appeal, advisory means giving an opinion to the President, and revisory means reviewing its own judgment.

assets.caption: The Court's main jurisdictions.

questions.stem_md: What does "original jurisdiction" of the Supreme Court mean?

options.text_md: Cases that come to it on appeal from lower courts
Questions referred to it by the President for its opinion
Cases in which it reconsiders its own earlier judgment
Cases that begin in the Supreme Court itself

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Cases that begin in the Supreme Court itself. Original jurisdiction covers cases that can be started directly in the Supreme Court. The other options describe appellate, advisory and review powers.

questions.stem_md: A High Court reverses the acquittal of an imagined accused and sentences him to death. To which court can he appeal, and under which kind of jurisdiction?

options.text_md: The Supreme Court, under its appellate jurisdiction in criminal cases
The President, under the original jurisdiction of the High Court
A District Court, under its advisory jurisdiction
The Lok Sabha, under its judicial powers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Supreme Court, under its appellate jurisdiction in criminal cases. Where a High Court reverses an acquittal and passes a death sentence, an appeal lies to the Supreme Court as of right in its criminal appellate jurisdiction. The President has mercy powers, not appellate jurisdiction; District Courts are below the High Court; the Lok Sabha does not hear criminal appeals.

questions.stem_md: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court may grant special leave to appeal against a judgment of almost any court or tribunal in India. Which body is outside this power?

options.text_md: A court or tribunal of the armed forces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A court or tribunal of the armed forces. Special leave to appeal can be granted against any court or tribunal except those constituted under laws relating to the armed forces. High Courts, District Courts and tax tribunals are within its reach.

questions.stem_md: Who can seek the advisory opinion of the Supreme Court under Article 143?

options.text_md: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The President. Only the President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion. Citizens, Governors and the Speaker have no such power.

questions.stem_md: An imagined President refers a question about a proposed law to the Supreme Court and receives its opinion. Which statement about that opinion is correct?

options.text_md: It guides the President but is not binding in the way a judgment is
It becomes a law as soon as it is published
It must be approved by the Lok Sabha before it is given
It can be given only after the law is passed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It guides the President but is not binding in the way a judgment is. An advisory opinion under Article 143 is advice; it is not a judgment in a dispute and does not bind the President in the way a decision binds parties. It does not become law, needs no Lok Sabha approval, and can be sought on a proposed measure.

questions.stem_md: A High Court certifies that a case before it involves a substantial question of law about the interpretation of the Constitution. Which appeal does this certificate allow?

options.text_md: An appeal to the President for mercy
A reference to the Election Commission
A fresh trial in a District Court
An appeal to the Supreme Court in a constitutional case

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** An appeal to the Supreme Court in a constitutional case. Such a certificate opens an appeal to the Supreme Court in its constitutional appellate jurisdiction. Mercy, the Election Commission and fresh trials are unrelated.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A dispute between the Union and a State can be taken directly to the Supreme Court.

**Reason (R):** The Supreme Court can hear appeals in civil cases from the High Courts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A rests on the original jurisdiction under Article 131; R is about appellate jurisdiction, which is a different power.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A private company can ask the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion on a new tax.

**Reason (R):** Under Article 143 the President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: only the President can seek an advisory opinion. R is true and states that rule.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined matter with the jurisdiction under which the Supreme Court deals with it.

options.text_md: Two States dispute a river-bank boundary road
A civil suit lost in a High Court is taken further
The President asks whether a proposed law is valid
The Court reconsiders its own earlier judgment

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Disputes between States begin in the Supreme Court (original); appeals from High Courts are appellate; the President's reference is advisory; reconsidering its own judgment is review under Article 137.

questions.stem_md: Name the kinds of disputes that fall within the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
questions.solution_md: The three combinations of Union and State parties under Article 131.

answer.model_answer_md: Disputes **between the Union and one or more States**; between the **Union and some States on one side and other States** on the other; and **between two or more States**.

questions.stem_md: Name two kinds of cases that can reach the Supreme Court under its appellate jurisdiction.
questions.solution_md: Any two of constitutional, civil, criminal and special-leave appeals with a brief qualifier.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Constitutional cases**, on a certificate that a **substantial question about the Constitution** is involved.
2. **Criminal cases**, for example where a High Court **reverses an acquittal** and passes a **death sentence**. (Also civil cases and appeals by **special leave**.)

questions.stem_md: Explain the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and why it is useful to the President.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, nature of the opinion, and usefulness.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Under **Article 143**, the **President** may refer a **question of law or fact of public importance** to the Supreme Court.
2. The Court considers it and **gives its opinion**, which **guides** the government but does **not bind** it like a judgment.
3. It is useful because the President and ministers can **check the legal position before acting**, avoiding later disputes about **constitutional validity**.

questions.stem_md: After a decision, an imagined party points out an error apparent on the face of the record and asks the Supreme Court to look at its own judgment again. Which power does the Court use?

options.text_md: Its power to review its own judgments (Article 137)
Its power to issue a writ of quo warranto

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Its power to review its own judgments (Article 137). Article 137 lets the Supreme Court review its own judgments or orders, for example to correct an obvious error. Advisory and original jurisdiction and quo warranto do not reopen its own decisions.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the judicial review power of the Supreme Court?

options.text_md: The power to examine laws and executive orders and declare them void if they violate the Constitution
The power to make new laws when Parliament is not in session
The power to review the budget every year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The power to examine laws and executive orders and declare them void if they violate the Constitution. Judicial review lets the Court test laws and orders against the Constitution and strike down those that conflict with it. Making laws, appointing ministers and reviewing the budget are not judicial functions.

questions.stem_md: An imagined State passes a law that forbids people of one religion from buying land anywhere in the State. A citizen challenges it. What can the Supreme Court do if it finds the law against the Fundamental Rights?

options.text_md: Only advise the Governor to reconsider the law
Declare the law unconstitutional and void, using its power of judicial review
Ask the Lok Sabha to vote on whether the law is fair
Do nothing, because State laws cannot be examined by courts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Declare the law unconstitutional and void, using its power of judicial review. Using judicial review, the Court can declare a law void to the extent it violates the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. Advice to the Governor or a Lok Sabha vote is not how the Court acts, and State laws are subject to review.

questions.stem_md: The Supreme Court is called a "Court of Record". What does this mean for its judgments?

options.text_md: It keeps a record of all citizens' property
It records the votes of Parliament
Its judgments are recorded for evidence and as precedents, and it can punish for contempt of itself
It records the oath of every minister

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its judgments are recorded for evidence and as precedents, and it can punish for contempt of itself. As a Court of Record (Article 129), its judgments and proceedings are preserved as evidence and precedent that cannot be questioned when produced in a court, and it has the power to punish for contempt. The other options describe unrelated records.

questions.stem_md: According to Article 141, the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on whom?

options.text_md: Only the High Court of Delhi
Only the parties to that case
All courts within the territory of India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** All courts within the territory of India. Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India. It is not limited to one High Court, the Union government or the parties.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Supreme Court is often described as the guardian of the Constitution.

**Reason (R):** Through judicial review, it can strike down laws and executive actions that violate the Constitution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true and R explains A: the power to invalidate unconstitutional laws and actions is what lets the Court protect the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because the Supreme Court is a Court of Record, it can punish a person for contempt of the Court.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Article 129 makes it a Court of Record with all the powers of such a court, including the power to punish for contempt of itself.

questions.stem_md: The Supreme Court's power to review its own judgments is given by Article ___ of the Constitution.
questions.solution_md: Article 137 gives the power of review.

questions.stem_md: Give two features of the Supreme Court as a Court of Record.
questions.solution_md: Records as evidence and precedent; contempt power.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Its **judgments and proceedings are recorded** and used as **evidence and precedents**, and cannot be questioned when produced in any court.
2. It has the power to **punish for contempt** of itself.

questions.stem_md: Why is judicial review important for protecting citizens in a democracy?
questions.solution_md: Limits on majorities; protection of rights.

answer.model_answer_md: It ensures that **even a majority in Parliament or a government cannot override the Constitution**; laws or orders that **violate Fundamental Rights** can be **struck down**, so citizens' rights stay protected.

marking_scheme.step: Limits on the legislature and executive

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the Supreme Court's power of judicial review and its power to review its own judgments.
questions.solution_md: Object of each power and the contrast.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Judicial review** tests **laws and executive actions** of Parliament, State legislatures and governments against the **Constitution**.
2. **Review of its own judgments (Article 137)** lets the Court **reconsider its own earlier decision**, for example to correct an **error apparent on the record**.
3. So the first checks **other organs**, while the second corrects the **Court itself**.

questions.stem_md: Ramesh, an imagined shopkeeper, is held by the police for five days without being produced before a magistrate. His sister petitions the Supreme Court. Which writ is most suitable?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Habeas corpus. Habeas corpus orders the authority to produce the detained person before the court so that the legality of the detention can be examined. Mandamus commands a duty, quo warranto questions a claim to a public office, and certiorari quashes an order of a lower court.

questions.stem_md: An imagined municipal officer refuses, without any legal reason, to issue a birth certificate that the law requires him to issue. Which writ commands him to do his duty?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Mandamus. Mandamus ("we command") orders a public authority to perform a public duty it is bound to perform. Habeas corpus concerns detention, prohibition is aimed at lower courts, and quo warranto at the right to hold an office.

questions.stem_md: Citizens find that the chairperson of an imagined State public body was appointed although she does not meet the age condition in the law creating the office. Which writ asks her by what authority she holds the office?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Quo warranto. Quo warranto ("by what authority") asks a person to show the legal authority for holding a public office and can remove a person not qualified for it. The other writs serve different purposes.

questions.stem_md: A lower tribunal is about to decide a case that the law places outside its powers, and the decision has not yet been given. Which writ stops it from going ahead?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Prohibition. Prohibition is issued before a decision, to stop a lower court or tribunal from acting beyond its jurisdiction. Certiorari is issued after an order is passed, to quash it. Mandamus and habeas corpus do not deal with jurisdiction of lower courts.

questions.stem_md: An imagined tribunal has already passed an order that it had no power to pass. Which writ can the higher court issue to quash that order?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Certiorari. Certiorari is issued after the order, to transfer the record and quash a decision made without jurisdiction or in clear violation of law. Prohibition would have been used before the decision.

questions.stem_md: Under which Article can a citizen move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Article 32. Article 32 gives the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcing Fundamental Rights, and itself is a Fundamental Right. Article 143 is advisory, 356 is President's Rule and 72 is the President's mercy power.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights is itself one of the Fundamental Rights.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Article 32 is in Part III of the Constitution, so the remedy is guaranteed as a Fundamental Right; Dr B. R. Ambedkar regarded it as among the most important provisions.

questions.stem_md: The writ that orders a person who has been detained to be produced before the court is called ___.
questions.solution_md: Habeas corpus means "you may have the body"; the detained person is produced before the court.

questions.stem_md: Match each writ with its purpose.

match_right.text_md: Ask by what authority a person holds a public office
Produce a detained person before the court
Quash an order already passed by a lower court without jurisdiction
Stop a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction before it decides
Command a public authority to perform its duty

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(t), (c)–(s), (d)–(r), (e)–(p). Each writ answers one kind of wrong: unlawful detention, neglect of duty, threatened excess of jurisdiction, completed excess of jurisdiction, and unlawful holding of office.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The writ of prohibition is issued before a lower court has delivered its decision.

**Reason (R):** The writ of prohibition can be issued against a private company to stop it from breaking a contract.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: prohibition lies against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies acting beyond their powers, not against private companies.

questions.stem_md: State the meaning of the writs of habeas corpus and mandamus.
questions.solution_md: One accurate meaning each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Habeas corpus:** an order to **produce a detained person** before the court so that the **lawfulness of the detention** can be tested.
**Mandamus:** an order to a **public authority** to **perform a public duty** it is legally bound to do.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the writs of prohibition and certiorari.
questions.solution_md: Timing and effect of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Prohibition** is issued **before** a lower court or tribunal decides, to **stop** it acting beyond its jurisdiction. **Certiorari** is issued **after** an order is passed, to **quash** an order made without jurisdiction.

questions.stem_md: Suggest the writ that an imagined citizen should seek in each case, with a reason: (a) a college principal holds office without the qualification the law requires; (b) a tribunal has passed an order beyond its powers; (c) an official refuses to issue a ration card the law entitles the citizen to.
questions.solution_md: One correct writ and reason for each case.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Quo warranto**, because it questions the **authority** by which the principal **holds a public office**.
(b) **Certiorari**, because the order is **already passed** and must be **quashed**.
(c) **Mandamus**, because it **commands the official** to perform a **legal duty**.

questions.stem_md:
A Class 10 student is preparing a talk on how the Supreme Court is staffed.

(i) State the composition of the Supreme Court and the qualifications of its judges. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the judges are appointed. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the grounds and procedure for removing a judge. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Composition and qualifications; appointment; removal.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Court has a **Chief Justice of India** and up to **33 other judges** (sanctioned strength **34**, as of 2024). A judge must be a **citizen** and must have been a **High Court judge for 5 years**, or an **advocate of a High Court for 10 years**, or a **distinguished jurist** in the President's opinion.

(ii) Judges are appointed by the **President**. In practice, names are **recommended by a collegium** of the Chief Justice and senior-most judges, a practice that grew from Supreme Court judgments in the **1990s**; the **senior-most judge** is usually made **Chief Justice**. A 2014 attempt to replace this with a commission (**NJAC**) was **struck down in 2015**.

(iii) A judge can be removed only for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**. A motion is moved in a House, an **inquiry committee** examines the charge, and **each House** must pass an **address** by a **majority of its total membership** and **two-thirds of members present and voting** in the same session. The **President** then orders the removal. Judges otherwise serve until **65**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the independence of the judiciary.

(i) Why is it important for the judiciary to be independent of the executive and the legislature? **[3]**
(ii) Explain any three provisions about tenure and salary that protect the judges. **[3]**
(iii) Explain any two other provisions that keep the Supreme Court independent, and say whether you think they are enough. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Importance; tenure and salary provisions; other provisions with a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Court decides **disputes involving the government**, protects **Fundamental Rights** and interprets the **Constitution**; judges must be able to decide **without fear or favour**, or citizens would lose trust in **justice**.

(ii) Judges serve until **65** (**security of tenure**); they can be removed only for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity** by a **special majority of both Houses**; their **salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund** and **cannot be cut** after appointment except in a **financial emergency**.

(iii) Parliament **cannot discuss a judge's conduct** except during removal, and the Court can **punish for contempt**; retired judges **cannot practise** in any court in India. These provisions together give **strong protection**; a balanced answer may add that **public trust** and **transparent appointments** also matter.

questions.stem_md:
Read the situation and answer. *(Imagined.)* In one year the Supreme Court hears a dispute between the Union and the State of Pashchimgarh, an appeal in a murder case from a High Court, and a question sent by the President.

(i) Name the jurisdiction used in each of the three matters. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the appellate jurisdiction, mentioning the kinds of appeals it covers. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Identification; original; appellate.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Union–State dispute: **original jurisdiction**; the murder appeal: **appellate jurisdiction (criminal)**; the President's question: **advisory jurisdiction**.

(ii) Under **Article 131**, cases that **begin in the Supreme Court**: disputes **between the Union and one or more States**, between the **Union and States on one side and other States** on the other, and **between States**. No other court can hear these.

(iii) It hears **appeals from High Courts** in **constitutional cases** (on a certificate of a substantial question about the Constitution), **civil cases** (substantial question of general importance), and **criminal cases** (for example where a High Court reverses an acquittal and passes a **death sentence**). Under **Article 136** it may grant **special leave to appeal** from almost any court or tribunal except **armed forces tribunals**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about some special powers of the Supreme Court.

(i) Explain the advisory jurisdiction of the Court. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the Court's power to review its own judgments. **[3]**
(iii) What is meant by a Court of Record? Explain two of its features. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Advisory; review; Court of Record.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Under **Article 143**, the **President** may refer a **question of law or fact of public importance**; the Court gives its **opinion**, which **guides** but does **not bind** like a judgment.

(ii) Under **Article 137**, the Court may **reconsider its own judgment or order**, for example to correct an **error apparent on the record**; this keeps its decisions **just** even after they are delivered.

(iii) A **Court of Record** is one whose **judgments and proceedings are preserved** as **evidence and precedent**. Its records **cannot be questioned** when produced in a court, and it has the power to **punish for contempt** of itself (**Article 129**).

questions.stem_md:
A citizen's group argues that judicial review makes the Supreme Court the protector of the Constitution.

(i) What is judicial review? **[3]**
(ii) Explain how judicial review protects Fundamental Rights and the federal division of powers. **[3]**
(iii) Give two arguments in favour of this power and one concern sometimes raised about it. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning; protection of rights and federalism; balanced arguments.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It is the power of the Court to **examine laws** passed by Parliament and State legislatures and **executive orders**, and to declare them **void** if they **violate the Constitution**.

(ii) A law that takes away a **Fundamental Right** beyond what the Constitution allows can be **struck down**; a law made by the **Union on a State subject** (or the reverse) outside its powers can be declared invalid, keeping the **federal balance**.

(iii) **For:** it protects **minorities and individuals** against majorities; it keeps every organ **within constitutional limits**. **Concern:** some argue that **unelected judges** may sometimes go too far into **policy decisions** best left to elected bodies; others respond that the Court acts only on **constitutional grounds**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

(i) Under which Article can a citizen go directly to the Supreme Court, and why is this right important? **[3]**
(ii) Explain the writs of habeas corpus, mandamus and quo warranto. **[3]**
(iii) Explain the writs of prohibition and certiorari, bringing out the difference between them. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Article 32 and its importance; three writs; two writs contrasted.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Article 32** gives the right to move the **Supreme Court** for enforcing **Fundamental Rights**; it is **itself a Fundamental Right**, so the rights are **not just promises** but can be **enforced**.

(ii) **Habeas corpus:** produce a **detained person** to test the detention. **Mandamus:** command a **public authority** to do its **legal duty**. **Quo warranto:** ask **by what authority** a person holds a **public office**.

(iii) **Prohibition** is issued to a lower court or tribunal **before** it decides, to **stop** it from going **beyond its jurisdiction**. **Certiorari** is issued **after** the order, to **quash** it. So prohibition **prevents** and certiorari **cures**.

questions.stem_md:
Compare and explain.

(i) Distinguish between original and appellate jurisdiction with one example of each. **[3]**
(ii) Compare the removal of a Supreme Court judge with the removal of the President on two points. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the Supreme Court acts as the final interpreter of the Constitution. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Two jurisdictions; two removals; final interpreter.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Original:** cases that **begin** in the Supreme Court, e.g. a **dispute between two States**. **Appellate:** cases that come **on appeal** from a **High Court**, e.g. an appeal in a **criminal case** where a death sentence is passed after reversal of an acquittal.

(ii) **Ground:** a judge for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**; the President for **violation of the Constitution**. **Majority:** a judge needs a **majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting** in each House; the President needs **two-thirds of the total membership** of each House.

(iii) Through **judicial review**, it decides whether laws and actions agree with the **Constitution**; under **Article 141** its rulings **bind all courts**; it **settles Union–State disputes**; and through **writs** and **appeals** its interpretation becomes **final**, subject only to the Constitution being amended within its limits.
